strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing noise and improving relevance in RAG for secure code generation, with clear identification of two concrete limitations (irrelevant code logic in retrieved examples, and lack of security semantics in retrieval).

Technically sound and creative combination of two distinct techniques: LLM-based cluster-then-summarize distillation for high-level guidelines and static program slicing (via PDG-based bidirectional slicing) for concise code examples, mapped onto a CWE-based hierarchical knowledge base.

The multi-faceted retrieval (vulnerability cause analysis, draft code/API pattern, code similarity) is a sensible way to inject security semantics that are not explicit in raw task descriptions, and the modified RRF fusion with thresholding is a reasonable design choice.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six LLMs, four benchmarks (including both a dedicated security benchmark and three functional-correctness benchmarks), and five strong/diverse baselines representing different paradigms (fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-augmented iterative refinement, RAG).

Proposes a new metric, SecurePass@k, that jointly evaluates security and functional correctness, addressing a real flaw in prior evaluation practice where methods can trivially inflate SecureRate by generating non-functional code (well illustrated by INDICT's results).

Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of knowledge base construction (guideline vs. slicing, retrieval-stage vs. generation-stage slicing) and of each retrieval facet, plus sensitivity analysis of the hierarchical retrieval parameter k.

Additional robustness checks are valuable: testing that gains are not simply due to using GPT-4o as summarizer (swapping in open-source models), overhead/timing breakdown, and CWE-distribution analysis for generalization beyond training vulnerability types.
Reasonable engineering detail and reproducibility support via appendices (algorithms for clustering/summarization and slicing, full prompt templates, dataset description).
weaknesses: Improvements over baselines are often modest and inconsistent across models: for Llama3.1-8B, RESCUE's Pass@1 and SR gains are small and BCB/LCB scores sometimes decrease relative to LLM alone or other baselines (e.g., Table 1 BCB/LCB numbers for GPT-4o-mini and Qwen-32B), raising questions about robustness of the claimed 4.8-point average gain across all settings.

The raw security dataset is small (704 instances, only ~9-12 CWE types per language in training), which may limit the diversity/coverage of the constructed knowledge base; while generalization to unseen CWE types is claimed (Appendix B.4), the analysis is fairly coarse (counts of CWE types, not per-type performance breakdown).

The paper does not report statistical significance or variance across the sampled generations (100 or 10 samples per problem), making it hard to assess whether reported differences (especially small ones, e.g., <1-2 points) are meaningful versus noise.

SecCoder baseline reimplementation reuses RESCUE's own retriever and raw security data 'for fair comparison', which could disadvantage the original SecCoder design and makes it harder to disentangle whether gains come from the proposed hierarchical/multi-faceted retrieval versus simply better underlying data/embedding choices.

The evaluation of Codexity and INDICT with a different security tool (semgrep instead of CodeQL) to avoid data leakage is reasonable in principle, but this changes the feedback signal quality for those baselines and could bias comparison against RESCUE, which never faces this substitution issue.

Overhead analysis (Appendix B.3) shows substantial added latency (e.g., ~24s extra per sample for DeepSeek-V3 due to draft generation + cause analysis + augmented generation), which is a real practical cost not deeply discussed in the main text or compared quantitatively against baseline methods' overhead (e.g., INDICT's iterative refinement).

The method requires an LLM (GPT-4o) for offline knowledge base construction and, more importantly, at least two additional LLM calls per inference (draft generation + vulnerability cause analysis) before final generation, which somewhat undercuts the 'training-free' framing relative to simpler RAG baselines and adds cost/complexity not fully quantified against baselines in terms of dollar/API cost.

Some presentation issues: Table 1 lacks clear indication of statistical variance; discussion of cases where RESCUE underperforms on Pass@1/BCB/LCB is limited, and the paper could more critically discuss when/why the method might fail (e.g., smaller models like Llama3.1-8B show weaker gains) rather than mostly reporting favorable aggregate numbers.

Novelty is somewhat incremental in the sense that it combines known techniques (program slicing, cluster-then-summarize, RRF, hierarchical taxonomy retrieval) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the core contribution is more of a careful systems-engineering integration than a conceptual breakthrough.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning six LLMs, four benchmarks, and five state-of-the-art baselines, which is a non-trivial experimental effort.

Introduces a reasonable new metric (SecurePass@1) that jointly captures security and functional correctness, addressing a real gap in prior evaluation practice where methods could trivially boost SecureRate by generating non-functional code.

The hybrid knowledge base construction (cluster-then-summarize plus PDG-based bidirectional slicing) is a sensible engineering combination that is shown via ablation (Table 2) to meaningfully reduce token length (~81.5%) and improve performance over using raw, unprocessed security data.

Extensive ablation studies (knowledge base components, hierarchy depth k, facet combinations, summarization model choice) support the individual design decisions rather than just reporting an end-to-end number.
Reasonable attempt to avoid data-leakage concerns by using different static analysis tools for baseline refinement (semgrep) versus evaluation (CodeQL).
weaknesses: The claim that RESCUE 'does not affect functional correctness' is not well supported: Table 1 and the aggregated Table 5 show non-trivial Pass@1 drops on BigCodeBench (avg -3.63) and inconsistent results on other benchmarks (e.g., GPT-4o-mini loses ~9 points of Pass@1 on BCB, and several models show notable HE+ drops). This functionality cost is understated in the main text relative to the security gains emphasized.

Gains in SecurePass@1 are modest and inconsistent across models (e.g., only ~2.5 points for Llama3.1-8B versus ~5+ for DeepSeek-V3/GPT-4o-mini), raising questions about the generality and practical significance of the proposed method across model families.

The method introduces substantial inference-time overhead (multiple LLM calls for draft generation, vulnerability-cause analysis, and augmented generation), which per Table 7 can add 10+ seconds per sample for larger models like DeepSeek-V3; this cost is acknowledged but not rigorously weighed against the modest accuracy gains, nor compared against baseline overheads (e.g., Codexity, INDICT) for a fair cost-benefit analysis.

Important recent RAG-based security baselines mentioned in the related work (SOSecure, PromSec) are not included in the empirical comparison, despite being the most directly comparable prior work; only SecCoder is used as the RAG baseline, weakening the claim of establishing a new state of the art among RAG approaches specifically.

The security knowledge base is built from a small, fixed dataset (704 instances, 9–12 CWE types per language), and while Appendix B.4 shows benchmark CWE coverage is broader, there is no fine-grained analysis of per-CWE-type performance or of how well the method handles truly unseen CWE categories versus those with partial overlap, making the generalizability claim somewhat superficial.

Key hyperparameters (facet thresholds 4.0/0.75/0.65, hop limit h=2, RRF parameters) appear to be manually tuned without a documented sensitivity analysis beyond k, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns.

No variance or statistical significance reporting is provided despite generating multiple samples per problem, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (sometimes only 1-2 points) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The 'hierarchical' framing is somewhat overstated, as the knowledge base has only two levels (CWE-level and code-level) and the retrieval correspondingly performs a two-step process, which is a relatively shallow hierarchy compared to the conceptual framing in the introduction.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: identifies two concrete, well-articulated limitations of naive RAG for secure code generation (irrelevant noise in retrieved documents, and lack of security-semantic retrieval beyond surface task descriptions).

Technically interesting hybrid knowledge base construction combining LLM-based cluster-then-summarize distillation with static program-dependence-graph slicing to produce both abstract guidelines and concise, security-focused code examples.

Hierarchical multi-faceted retrieval design (CWE-level then code-level, fusing API pattern, vulnerability-cause, and code-similarity facets via a modified RRF) is a reasonable and non-trivial extension over single-signal dense retrieval baselines.

Introduces a new metric, SecurePass@k, that jointly accounts for functional correctness and security, addressing a real and demonstrated flaw in prior SecureRate-only evaluation (some baselines trivially inflate security by sacrificing functionality).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 LLMs across different families/sizes, 4 benchmarks (including a contamination-resistant one, LiveCodeBench), and 5 competitive baselines spanning fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-based iterative refinement, agentic debate, and RAG approaches.

Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions of guideline extraction, program slicing (with fine-grained retrieval-only vs generation-only variants), hierarchical depth (k), and each retrieval facet, which substantiate the design choices.

Additional robustness checks: impact of different summarization LLMs (showing gains are not merely due to GPT-4o), CWE distribution analysis showing generalization to unseen vulnerability types, and a computational overhead breakdown.
Clear writing and mostly reproducible methodology, with detailed appendices including algorithms and full prompt templates.
weaknesses: Improvements are inconsistent across models/benchmarks: for several LLMs (e.g., Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on BigCodeBench/HumanEval+), RESCUE's functional correctness (Pass@1) drops noticeably relative to the vanilla LLM, which somewhat undercuts the claim that functionality is preserved.

The security knowledge base is built from a fairly small and narrow source (704 instances from SafeCoder, limited to Python/C/C++), raising questions about scalability and coverage to other languages or more diverse vulnerability classes.

Key hyperparameters (facet thresholds τ for API/vulnerability-cause/code, RRF α, top-k=4, 2-hop slicing) appear to be manually tuned without a reported sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about generalizability and potential overfitting to the evaluation benchmarks.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided, particularly concerning since BigCodeBench/LiveCodeBench results rely on only 10 samples per problem, which may be noisy given the reported small deltas.

The novelty is primarily an engineering synthesis of existing techniques (RAG, program slicing, CWE taxonomy, LLM summarization) rather than a fundamentally new technical idea; the core contribution is incremental relative to SecCoder/SOSecure despite empirical improvements.

Limited qualitative/error analysis: the paper does not deeply investigate cases where slicing removes important context or where multi-facet retrieval still fails, beyond aggregate LoC reduction statistics.

Baselines may not be perfectly comparable in all cases (e.g., SecCoder uses the same retriever and raw data but not the authors' curated knowledge base; Codexity and INDICT rely on different underlying security tools), which could affect the fairness of some comparisons despite the authors' efforts to control for data leakage.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 6 LLMs (open and closed source, various sizes), 4 benchmarks (CodeGuard+, HumanEval+, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench), and 5 diverse state-of-the-art baselines representing different paradigms (fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-based refinement, agentic debate, RAG).

Identifies and addresses a real gap in prior evaluation practice: many secure-code baselines trade off functional correctness for security, and the proposed SecurePass@k metric meaningfully captures this joint requirement, with supporting analysis (Table 5, Appendix C.1) showing other methods regress on Pass@1.

The two-part method (LLM-assisted cluster-then-summarize distillation + PDG-based bidirectional program slicing to build a hierarchical KB; multi-faceted CWE-level and code-level retrieval fusing API pattern/vulnerability-cause/code-similarity signals via a modified RRF) is reasonably well-motivated and clearly described with algorithmic detail in the appendix.

Extensive ablations and robustness checks: knowledge-base construction ablations, hierarchical retrieval depth (k) sweep, per-facet retrieval ablation, sensitivity analysis of RRF thresholds, and sanity checks that gains aren't merely due to GPT-4o as summarizer (Table 4) or artifacts of static-analysis evaluation tools (CWEval dynamic benchmark, Appendix C.4).

Additional generalizability analyses (seen vs. unseen CWE types, cross-language transfer to Go/JavaScript) and an overhead/latency breakdown add credibility and practical context beyond headline numbers.

Data leakage concerns are explicitly considered when constructing baselines (e.g., using semgrep instead of CodeQL for Codexity), which is a thoughtful methodological detail often overlooked in similar work.
weaknesses: The magnitude and consistency of improvements are uneven across models: gains on Llama3.1-8B are small (SecurePass@1 56.2 vs. CoSec's 53.9, a modest margin), and RESCUE sometimes underperforms the base LLM or baselines on plain Pass@1 for HumanEval+/BigCodeBench/LiveCodeBench (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite HE+ drops from 73.0 to 70.4; GPT-4o-mini HE+ drops from 80.7 to 77.3), suggesting the functional-correctness preservation claim is not uniformly supported.

The core technical contribution is largely a careful combination/engineering of existing ideas (LLM summarization, program slicing, multi-facet dense+sparse retrieval, RRF fusion) rather than a fundamentally new retrieval or generation mechanism; novelty is incremental relative to SecCoder/SOSecure/PromSec-style RAG security work.

The security knowledge base is built from only 704 vulnerability-fix instances (372 Python, 332 C/C++) drawn from a single prior dataset (SafeCoder), raising concerns about coverage/bias; while cross-CWE and cross-language generalization experiments partially mitigate this, the fundamental scope is narrow (2-3 languages, limited vulnerability variety) compared to real-world CWE diversity.

Baseline comparisons are not fully uniform: SafeCoder and CoSec could only be applied to a subset of models due to resource/architecture constraints, which weakens the completeness of the six-model, five-baseline comparison matrix and makes some "state-of-the-art" claims apply only to partial subsets.

The pipeline is computationally heavy in the online stage (draft generation + vulnerability cause analysis + API extraction + two-level retrieval, each involving separate LLM calls), and although overhead is analyzed and argued to be acceptable, no wall-clock end-to-end comparison against baselines (e.g., Codexity/INDICT's iterative refinement) is given, making it hard to judge relative efficiency trade-offs.

Statistical significance/variance across the 100 (or 10) generation samples is not reported (e.g., confidence intervals or variance across runs), making it harder to assess whether some of the smaller reported gains (a few points) are robust versus noise.

The reliance on an LLM (GPT-4o or others) to produce "security guidelines" and "vulnerability causes" during offline distillation introduces a potential source of hallucinated or inaccurate security advice that is not directly validated by human security experts, despite the robustness check against different summarization models.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 6 LLMs (closed and open source, multiple sizes), 4 benchmarks (CodeGuard+, HumanEval+, BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench), and 5 competitive baselines representing distinct strategies (fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-based refinement, agentic debate, RAG).

Identification of a genuine evaluation gap (SecureRate ignoring functional correctness) and proposal of a combined SecurePass@k metric is a useful methodological contribution for the secure-code-generation literature.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (knowledge base construction components, hierarchical retrieval depth, facet combinations, RRF fusion strategy, threshold sensitivity) that attempt to isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Additional robustness analyses in the appendix are a plus: evaluation on a dynamic-testing benchmark (CWEval) to address static-analysis bias, seen/unseen CWE breakdown, and cross-language transfer (Go/JavaScript) despite the knowledge base being built only from Python/C/C++ data.
Clear and detailed methodological descriptions (PDG-based slicing algorithm, cluster-then-summarize pipeline, prompts) that aid reproducibility, with code reportedly released.
weaknesses: Functional correctness (Pass@1) frequently degrades noticeably relative to the LLM-alone baseline in several configurations (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-32B drops from 88.3 to 80.6 on CodeGuard+, GPT-4o-mini from 80.7 to 77.3, DeepSeek-V3 from 87.4 to 83.5), which is downplayed by reporting an aggregate '98.7% retained' figure that masks these larger per-model losses.

Gains on several benchmarks/models are small or inconsistent (e.g., LiveCodeBench results are essentially flat or mixed across models, BigCodeBench Pass@1 often decreases), raising concerns about the generality and robustness of the claimed improvements.

No statistical significance testing or variance/confidence intervals are reported anywhere despite sampling-based metrics (100 samples for CodeGuard+/HumanEval+, 10 for the larger benchmarks), making it hard to assess whether reported deltas (including the headline 4.8-point average) are robust or within noise.

The knowledge base is built from a small corpus (704 raw instances, 372 Python + 332 C/C++), which limits the diversity of distilled guidelines and code examples; the cross-language/unseen-CWE generalization claims, while interesting, rest on speculative mechanistic explanations (e.g., 'activating parametric knowledge') rather than rigorous analysis.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core ingredients (CWE-taxonomy-based hierarchy, LLM summarization, program slicing for context pruning, multi-aspect/proactive query generation, RRF fusion) are each individually well-established techniques; the contribution is primarily a careful combination/engineering of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new technique, and the paper's own related work shows closely related RAG-for-security approaches (SecCoder, SOSecure, Tony et al. 2025).

Ablation results sometimes contradict the paper's own narrative — e.g., Table 3 shows the full three-facet retrieval is NOT the best configuration for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (VA-only facet achieves higher SP@1 and Pass@1), and the 'w/o guideline' ablation shows negligible or even slightly positive effects of removing guidelines for some models — weakening the claimed necessity of all components.

The system introduces substantial additional complexity and inference overhead (multiple proactive LLM calls for draft generation, vulnerability-cause analysis, hierarchical retrieval) which is non-trivial (e.g., ~30+ seconds of extra latency for DeepSeek-V3 per task), and the baseline comparisons are incomplete since SafeCoder/CoSec could only be applied to a subset of open-source models due to resource constraints, limiting the fairness and completeness of cross-method comparisons.

Evaluation of security still relies heavily on automated static tools (CodeQL) and unit tests, which the paper itself acknowledges are imperfect (false positives/negatives); while CWEval is used as a partial dynamic-testing check, this is restricted to a small subset and does not fully address the concern of evaluation validity for the main results.

strengths: Clearly motivated problem: identifies two concrete limitations of prior RAG-for-security work (noisy raw documents, lack of security semantics in task descriptions) and proposes targeted solutions for each.

Technically interesting hybrid knowledge base construction combining LLM cluster-then-summarize distillation with PDG-based bidirectional program slicing to produce concise, security-focused artifacts at two levels of abstraction (CWE-level guidelines and code-level examples).

Hierarchical multi-faceted retrieval (API pattern, vulnerability cause, code similarity) with a thoughtfully modified RRF fusion (thresholding + rank filtering) is a sensible design that is empirically validated against single-facet and standard RRF variants.

Introduces a new metric, SecurePass@1, that jointly captures functional correctness and security, addressing a real gap where prior methods inflate SecureRate by sacrificing functionality — this is a useful contribution to the evaluation methodology of the sub-area.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 6 LLMs across different families/sizes, 4 benchmarks, 5 strong and diverse baselines (fine-tuning, decoding control, tool-based refinement, agentic debate, RAG), with consistent average gains in SecurePass@1.

Thorough ablation and analysis suite: knowledge base components (guideline vs. slicing), hierarchical retrieval depth (k sweep), facet combinations (all 7 subsets), RRF strategy and threshold sensitivity, robustness to summarization LLM choice, computational overhead breakdown, generalization to unseen CWEs and unseen programming languages, and validation on an independent dynamic-testing benchmark (CWEval) to rule out static-analysis-tool artifacts.
Good reproducibility support: detailed algorithms in appendix, full prompt templates, code release, and a clear reproducibility/limitations/ethics statement.
weaknesses: Functional correctness (Pass@1) sometimes degrades noticeably under RESCUE relative to the base LLM (e.g., BigCodeBench Pass@1 drops for several models, HumanEval+ drops for GPT-4o-mini and Llama3.1-8B), which somewhat undercuts the claim that RESCUE preserves functional correctness, even though SecurePass@1 improves.

Gains are inconsistent and sometimes small for certain models (e.g., Llama3.1-8B shows only modest SecurePass@1 improvement and lower Pass@1 than several baselines), suggesting the method's benefit may be model-dependent and not uniformly strong.

The modified RRF introduces several additional hyperparameters (per-facet thresholds τ_i, smoothing α, top-k) whose sensitivity analysis is conducted on a very small validation subset (20 instances, 2 models), which is somewhat thin evidence for robustness claims.

The knowledge base is built from a relatively small, English/Python/C/C++-centric dataset (704 instances); claims of cross-language and cross-CWE generalization, while supported by additional experiments, still rely on a narrow source distribution and a single external benchmark (CWEval) for validation.

The pipeline is computationally heavy at inference time (draft generation, vulnerability-cause analysis, two-stage retrieval, augmented generation each requiring separate LLM calls), and although overhead is discussed, the practical cost-benefit tradeoff versus simpler baselines (e.g., SecCoder) is not deeply analyzed in terms of latency-adjusted performance.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided despite generating multiple samples per problem, making it harder to assess whether some of the more marginal improvements are robust.

Baseline fairness is only partially addressed (e.g., different security tools used for Codexity to avoid leakage, SafeCoder/CoSec restricted to subsets of models), which, while reasonably justified, somewhat limits the strict comparability of results across all methods and models.
